=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel – Buyer-Side Review of Seller SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

**To:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Re:** Seller's "Key Negotiated Positions" and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)
**Date:** 5 November 2026

## Preliminary point: the "Reviewer Efficiency Note"

Before the substance, one flag. The Seller's package instructs the reviewer to treat all clauses marked [STANDARD] as "reviewed and cleared by both sides" and to proceed on the basis that the Buyer has "already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package". Nothing in our instructions supports that. Every clause tagged [STANDARD] is in fact a Seller-favourable position on a contested point, and none is marked [OPEN]. I have disregarded the note and reviewed everything. You should confirm with Seller's counsel in writing that no clause is agreed until we say so, so this labelling cannot later be pointed to as a course-of-dealing concession.

Also note the disclosure letter's own paragraph 11: the Seller expressly says the Buyer must evaluate the facts itself. The disclosure letter and the cover note are internally inconsistent on this.

---

## 1. Liability package (cl 12.1–12.3, 13)

**Seller position:** 20% cap (AUD 4.8m); de minimis AUD 25k; basket AUD 250k, *excess-only* recovery; 18-month claims period; limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly carved out.

**Analysis:**
- A 20% cap with no W&I insurance is at the low end for a sub-AUD 50m Australian private deal where the Seller is a venture holder (likely to distribute proceeds). The identified known exposures alone (Riverlark AUD 3.2m, bonuses AUD 420k, Ironquay AUD 180k, Sandbar AUD 330k, unquantified privacy incident) approach the cap before any unknown warranty issue is counted. If known matters are not stripped out and dealt with separately (see below), the cap is illusory.
- "Excess only" (deductible) basket should be "tipping" (first-dollar once exceeded). Basket at ~1% of price is acceptable; de minimis at AUD 25k is slightly high for a business with AUD ~12m revenue — push to AUD 10–15k, and ensure related claims aggregate.
- 18 months is short for a September/October completion: it means the Buyer may not have a full post-completion audit cycle. Push for 24 months minimum for general warranties.
- The "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" default must be reversed: carve-outs must be express and comprehensive (see item 2).

**Recommendation:** Cap 50–100% of price for general warranties (settle at 30–40% if trading for other concessions); tipping basket; 24 months general; aggregate related claims; and strip known issues into indemnities outside the cap/basket.

## 2. Fundamental / title warranties subjected to general caps

**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties capped and time-limited like general warranties "for administrative simplicity".

**Analysis:** This is a material departure from market and from buyer interest. If the Seller does not actually own the shares, the Buyer's recovery would be capped at 20% of what it paid, and lost after 18 months. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason. Title, capacity, authority and solvency warranties should be capped at 100% of price and run for the longest permitted period (6–7 years, or indefinitely subject to statute).

**Recommendation:** Reject outright. Fundamental warranties: 100% cap, 6+ years. Tax warranties: 100% cap (or at least separate cap), 7 years / statutory amendment period + 6 months.

## 3. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

**Analysis:** Tax warranties should sit outside the general regime (longer period, higher cap, and ideally a separate pre-Completion tax indemnity on a pound-for-pound basis). IP is the core asset of an analytics business; the Ironquay issue (item 8) shows IP title is not clean. IP warranties should have at least an extended period (3 years) and the Ironquay matter a specific indemnity.

**Recommendation:** Separate tax indemnity; tax warranties 7 years; IP warranties extended period and cap.

## 4. Limitations / exclusive remedy / non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3, 12.8, 20.5)

**Analysis:** As drafted, the caps and exclusive remedy would also cover: specific indemnities, the Riverlark release obligation, the Bluefen condition, Completion undertakings, leakage claims (if any), restraint breaches, and — critically — fraud and wilful misconduct. Limitation of liability for fraud is unenforceable as a matter of public policy, but a blanket clause invites argument. The non-reliance clause should not extend to the Disclosure Letter, the Accounts, or the Seller's written responses to DD questions. Note also Australian Consumer Law s 18 (misleading or deceptive conduct) cannot be contracted out of; a non-reliance clause may be relevant to causation but we should not concede any language purporting to exclude it.

**Recommendation:** Carve out from all limitations: fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment; specific indemnities; Completion deliverables and covenants (Riverlark, Bluefen); fundamental and tax warranties; leakage. Exclusive-remedy clause not to prejudice equitable remedies (injunction/specific performance) or statutory rights.

## 5. Disclosure framework (Sch 7, Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2, 1.4)

**Seller position:** General disclosure of the entire data room (DD-002 to DD-012), statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records", disclosure qualifying warranties generally.

**Analysis:**
- General disclosure of an entire data room is a common seller ask but should only be accepted with a "fair disclosure" standard: disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. The Disclosure Letter repeatedly says the material "does not state" or "does not establish" things (paras 5, 6, 8) — that is the Seller conceding its own disclosure is incomplete, which under a fair-disclosure standard means those matters are *not* disclosed against the warranties.
- "Publicly searchable corporate records" is open-ended (ASIC, PPSR, court lists, IP Australia, land titles, OAIC?). Limit to specified searches on specified dates, annexed.
- Paragraph 1.4 (no admission that any consent/payment/notice is required) is fine as a non-admission, but we need the converse: a Buyer non-waiver — acknowledging a disclosure does not accept it is adequate or that the matter is not a breach.
- Data room cut-off of 22 September 2026 — we are now six weeks on. Require a bring-down disclosure at Completion with disclosure against Completion-date warranties restricted to matters arising in the ordinary course, with a Buyer walk right for material new disclosures.

**Recommendation:** Fair-disclosure standard; data room index annexed and frozen; specific disclosures listed by warranty; limited public searches; Buyer non-waiver; bring-down regime with walk right.

## 6. Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3)

**Seller position:** No claim for any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records".

**Analysis:** This is the most aggressive clause in the package. Combined with general data-room disclosure, it effectively means the Buyer cannot claim on anything that could theoretically have been found. "Discoverable" is a constructive-knowledge standard — it is not what the Buyer knew but what a diligent adviser might have unearthed anywhere. It would also extinguish claims on exactly the issues listed in the Disclosure Letter (Riverlark, Ironquay, bonuses, privacy incident), because the Buyer now "knows" of them — while the Seller simultaneously refuses to quantify or indemnify them.

**Recommendation:** Delete. If a knowledge qualifier is to be conceded at all, limit to actual knowledge of three or four named Buyer deal-team individuals, of facts which they actually appreciated constituted a breach, and expressly exclude anything the subject of a specific indemnity. Advisers' knowledge is not to be imputed.

## 7. Bluefen consent (cl 3, 6.3; DL para 2)

**Facts:** Bluefen ≈ AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30% of FY26. Change-of-control consent required (cl 11.2), with conditions in cl 11.3. No final written consent and no evidence conditions are satisfied.

**Seller position:** "Addressed"; reasonable endeavours; condition satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent".

**Analysis:** 30% of revenue is existential for the valuation. The Seller's cover note says the matter is addressed; the Disclosure Letter says consent has not been obtained. "Reasonable endeavours" is the lowest standard. "Satisfied on delivery of written consent" ignores the 11.3 conditions — if Bluefen's consent is conditional (e.g. price re-opener, exclusivity, key personnel retention) the condition would be deemed satisfied while the commercial problem remains.

**Recommendation:** Condition precedent in Buyer's favour: unconditional written consent from Bluefen (or consent on conditions acceptable to Buyer acting reasonably), with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived in writing, and no notice of termination/renegotiation. Seller to use best (or all reasonable) endeavours; Buyer involvement in communications. Consider a price adjustment or earn-out component referable to Bluefen revenue retention for 12 months. Long-stop date with Buyer termination right.

## 8. Riverlark facility (cl 2, 7; DL para 3)

**Facts:** ≈ AUD 3.2m outstanding; change-of-control clause 8.1; security discharge 9.2. Not repaid; no discharge.

**Seller position:** Release "to be provided following Completion".

**Analysis:** This is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal. If the Buyer completes while AUD 3.2m is outstanding and secured over the Company's assets, the Buyer has paid AUD 24m for a company carrying AUD 3.2m of debt — 13% of price — and the bank has a change-of-control default from the moment of Completion. A post-Completion release relies on the Seller's good faith after it has the money. If this is the Seller's deliberate position, it is effectively a AUD 3.2m price increase.

**Recommendation:** Riverlark must be repaid from the purchase price at Completion via the funds flow (payoff letter from Riverlark delivered pre-Completion, with deed of release and PPSR discharge executed in escrow and released on payment). Debt-free adjustment to confirm. If the Seller refuses, this is a walk-away or price-reduction point.

## 9. Funds flow and DD-005 bonuses

**Facts:** AUD 420,000 of Completion bonuses, triggered by Completion and continued employment; not in the funds flow; on-costs (super, payroll tax) not addressed.

**Seller position:** "A matter for the Seller", not itemised.

**Analysis:** The bonuses are the Company's liabilities payable after Completion, i.e. the Buyer's cost unless adjusted. The "continued employment" condition means they probably crystallise post-Completion, when the Company is owned by the Buyer. With superannuation (12% from 1 July 2025) and NSW payroll tax (~5.45%) the true cost is roughly AUD 490–500k. If it is genuinely "a matter for the Seller", the Seller should pay it.

**Recommendation:** Treat as debt-like item in the completion accounts (grossed up for super, payroll tax and any PAYG), or Seller-funded through the funds flow at Completion. Specific indemnity for any shortfall. Confirm the bonus terms don't include further retention/change-of-control triggers.

## 10. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DL para 4)

**Facts:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, SOW3 Project Materials transfer only on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open. No payment receipt or confirmatory assignment in the data room.

**Seller position:** Indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment; "adequate".

**Analysis:** The exposure is not AUD 180k. Until the fees are paid, the Company does not own the SOW3 deliverables. If those materials are embedded in the Company's analytics product, the Company is using IP it does not own — an infringement risk, a licensing-out problem for customers (including Bluefen), and a hole in the IP title warranty. The indemnity needs to cover the consequences, not just the invoice.

**Recommendation:** Completion deliverable: evidence of cleared payment to Ironquay plus a confirmatory IP assignment (and moral rights consents) from Ironquay. Payment from Seller's proceeds. Indemnity extended to all loss arising from any failure of IP to vest, uncapped or separately capped, outside the basket. IP warranty that all Company IP is owned/validly licensed, unqualified by this disclosure.

## 11. Privacy incident (cl 4.6, Sch 6; DL para 6)

**Facts:** Download link sent to an unintended external address; ~1,240 records of personal information (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). Unknown whether accessed; investigation preliminary; six weeks old.

**Seller position:** "Preliminary operational matter", not material.

**Analysis:** Under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, the entity must assess a suspected eligible data breach within 30 days of becoming aware of it. The incident was disclosed as at 22 September; it is now 5 November — the 30-day assessment window has lapsed. If the assessment concluded serious harm is likely, notification to the OAIC and affected individuals is mandatory. The Seller's material "does not establish" whether notification is required — which suggests the assessment has not been completed or not been disclosed. Post-2024 reforms, OAIC has a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy and increased civil penalties (up to AUD 50m for serious interferences). The affected individuals also appear to be users of the Company's platform — i.e. customer-side data, raising contractual breach-notification obligations under customer contracts (very likely including Bluefen).

**Recommendation:** Require immediate production of the completed assessment; confirmation whether OAIC/individual/customer notifications were made; forensic evidence of non-access if relied upon. Specific indemnity for all loss arising from the DD-006 incident (regulatory, third-party, notification costs, customer claims), uncapped or capped at price, outside the basket, 6 years. Specific warranty of compliance with Privacy Act and customer data obligations. If notification obligations were missed, that is a current breach of law and should be remediated before Completion.

## 12. Sandbar supplier renewals (DL para 8)

**Facts:** Three related renewals, AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330k), split across DD-008 and DD-011; the Seller does not say whether they are accrued, terminable or ordinary course.

**Analysis:** Three identical amounts across two documents is a pattern worth probing — either a single arrangement deliberately split (below a materiality or approval threshold?) or related-party. The Buyer needs to know if these are committed liabilities at Completion (debt-like / working capital) or genuinely recurring opex priced into the valuation.

**Recommendation:** DD follow-up: copies of all three contracts, counterparties' ownership, approval history. If accrued or non-cancellable at Completion, include in completion-accounts adjustment. Seller warranty that no related-party arrangements exist other than as listed.

## 13. Office lease (DL para 7) and Mossvale (DL para 9)

- **Lease:** a notification obligation is still a Completion deliverable — require evidence it is given, and a warranty that the lease contains no change-of-control termination right. Verify directly.
- **Mossvale:** the Seller's drafting ("does not state consent is required merely because shares are sold") is careful. Review DD-009 ourselves for any change-of-control or "deemed assignment" language; many Australian contracts treat change of control as assignment. Add to the list of contracts for a Seller warranty of no change-of-control triggers.

## 14. Title (DL para 10)

**Analysis:** The share register is prima facie evidence of title under the *Corporations Act 2001* (Cth), but it is not conclusive and the Seller is at pains to say the Buyer has not verified it. The Seller's wish to cap title warranties (item 2) sits uneasily with this. Independent verification needed: ASIC company extract (current members, no charges/PPSR registrations over the shares), copy of the share certificate(s), constitution (pre-emptive rights, transfer restrictions), any shareholders' agreement, options/convertible notes, and historical transfers to Harbourglass.

**Recommendation:** Complete those searches now. Full-cap, long-period title warranty (item 2) is non-negotiable.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Priority | Position |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Riverlark AUD 3.2m | **Critical** | Repay at Completion from price; payoff letter and release in escrow. Not negotiable. |
| 2 | Bluefen consent (30% revenue) | **Critical** | Buyer CP: unconditional consent with 11.3 conditions satisfied; best endeavours; long-stop; consider retention earn-out. |
| 3 | Fundamental/title/tax warranties capped at 20%/18 months | **Critical** | Reject. 100% cap; 6–7 years. |
| 4 | Buyer knowledge cl 8.3 ("discoverable") | **Critical** | Delete; at most actual knowledge of named individuals, excluding indemnified matters. |
| 5 | Privacy incident | **High** | Completed NDB assessment and notification status now; uncapped specific indemnity. |
| 6 | Ironquay IP | **High** | Pay and obtain confirmatory assignment pre-Completion; indemnity for loss of IP, not just AUD 180k. |
| 7 | Bonuses AUD 420k + on-costs | **High** | Debt-like item / Seller-funded; indemnity for shortfall. |
| 8 | General limitations (cap, excess basket, 18 months, applies to all Claims) | **High** | Cap ≥30–50%; tipping basket; 24 months; express carve-outs for fraud, indemnities, covenants, fundamental/tax. |
| 9 | Disclosure framework | **High** | Fair-disclosure standard; frozen annexed index; limited searches; Buyer non-waiver; bring-down with walk right. |
| 10 | Sandbar renewals | Medium | Contracts and approvals; adjust if accrued; related-party warranty. |
| 11 | Lease / Mossvale | Medium | Verify change-of-control provisions ourselves; Completion deliverables. |
| 12 | Title verification | Medium | ASIC/PPSR/constitution checks now. |
| 13 | "Efficiency note" / [STANDARD] labels | Process | Record in writing that nothing is agreed; all clauses open. |

**Overall:** The identified known exposures (Riverlark AUD 3.2m, bonuses ~AUD 0.5m, Sandbar AUD 0.33m, Ironquay AUD 0.18m, plus an unquantified privacy matter) total upwards of AUD 4.2m against a AUD 4.8m general cap — the Seller's proposal would leave essentially no protection for unknown risks while inviting the Buyer to absorb the known ones. Our mark-up should (i) move every known matter into price adjustments, Completion deliverables or specific indemnities outside the cap, and (ii) restore market-standard warranty protection for the unknowns. If the Seller holds the Riverlark and Bluefen positions, those are price or walk-away issues, not drafting issues.

Happy to turn this into a mark-up of the SPA and a written response to Seller's counsel on your instructions.

**Recommendation:** Fair-disclosure standard; data room index annexed and frozen; specific disclosures listed by warranty; limited public searches; Buyer non-waiver; bring-down regime with walk right.

## 6. Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3)

**Seller position:** No claim for any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records".

**Analysis:** This is the most aggressive clause in the package. Combined with general data-room disclosure, it effectively means the Buyer cannot claim on anything that could theoretically have been found. "Discoverable" is a constructive-knowledge standard — it is not what the Buyer knew but what a diligent adviser might have unearthed anywhere. It would also extinguish claims on exactly the issues listed in the Disclosure Letter (Riverlark, Ironquay, bonuses, privacy incident), because the Buyer now "knows" of them — while the Seller simultaneously refuses to quantify or indemnify them.

**Recommendation:** Delete. If a knowledge qualifier is to be conceded at all, limit to actual knowledge of three or four named Buyer deal-team individuals, of facts which they actually appreciated constituted a breach, and expressly exclude anything the subject of a specific indemnity. Advisers' knowledge is not to be imputed.

## 7. Bluefen consent (cl 3, 6.3; DL para 2)

**Facts:** Bluefen ≈ AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30% of FY26. Change-of-control consent required (cl 11.2), with conditions in cl 11.3. No final written consent and no evidence conditions are satisfied.

**Seller position:** "Addressed"; reasonable endeavours; condition satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent".

**Analysis:** 30% of revenue is existential for the valuation. The Seller's cover note says the matter is addressed; the Disclosure Letter says consent has not been obtained. "Reasonable endeavours" is the lowest standard. "Satisfied on delivery of written consent" ignores the 11.3 conditions — if Bluefen's consent is conditional (e.g. price re-opener, exclusivity, key personnel retention) the condition would be deemed satisfied while the commercial problem remains.

**Recommendation:** Condition precedent in Buyer's favour: unconditional written consent from Bluefen (or consent on conditions acceptable to Buyer acting reasonably), with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived in writing, and no notice of termination/renegotiation. Seller to use best (or all reasonable) endeavours; Buyer involvement in communications. Consider a price adjustment or earn-out component referable to Bluefen revenue retention for 12 months. Long-stop date with Buyer termination right.

## 8. Riverlark facility (cl 2, 7; DL para 3)

**Facts:** ≈ AUD 3.2m outstanding; change-of-control clause 8.1; security discharge 9.2. Not repaid; no discharge.

**Seller position:** Release "to be provided following Completion".

**Analysis:** This is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal. If the Buyer completes while AUD 3.2m is outstanding and secured over the Company's assets, the Buyer has paid AUD 24m for a company carrying AUD 3.2m of debt — 13% of price — and the bank has a change-of-control default from the moment of Completion. A post-Completion release relies on the Seller's good faith after it has the money. If this is the Seller's deliberate position, it is effectively a AUD 3.2m price increase.

**Recommendation:** Riverlark must be repaid from the purchase price at Completion via the funds flow (payoff letter from Riverlark delivered pre-Completion, with deed of release and PPSR discharge executed in escrow and released on payment). Debt-free adjustment to confirm. If the Seller refuses, this is a walk-away or price-reduction point.

## 9. Funds flow and DD-005 bonuses

**Facts:** AUD 420,000 of Completion bonuses, triggered by Completion and continued employment; not in the funds flow; on-costs (super, payroll tax) not addressed.

**Seller position:** "A matter for the Seller", not itemised.

**Analysis:** The bonuses are the Company's liabilities payable after Completion, i.e. the Buyer's cost unless adjusted. The "continued employment" condition means they probably crystallise post-Completion, when the Company is owned by the Buyer. With superannuation (12% from 1 July 2025) and NSW payroll tax (~5.45%) the true cost is roughly AUD 490–500k. If it is genuinely "a matter for the Seller", the Seller should pay it.

**Recommendation:** Treat as debt-like item in the completion accounts (grossed up for super, payroll tax and any PAYG), or Seller-funded through the funds flow at Completion. Specific indemnity for any shortfall. Confirm the bonus terms don't include further retention/change-of-control triggers.

## 10. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DL para 4)

**Facts:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, SOW3 Project Materials transfer only on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open. No payment receipt or confirmatory assignment in the data room.

**Seller position:** Indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment; "adequate".

**Analysis:** The exposure is not AUD 180k. Until the fees are paid, the Company does not own the SOW3 deliverables. If those materials are embedded in the Company's analytics product, the Company is using IP it does not own — an infringement risk, a licensing-out problem for customers (including Bluefen), and a hole in the IP title warranty. The indemnity needs to cover the consequences, not just the invoice.

**Recommendation:** Completion deliverable: evidence of cleared payment to Ironquay plus a confirmatory IP assignment (and moral rights consents) from Ironquay. Payment from Seller's proceeds. Indemnity extended to all loss arising from any failure of IP to vest, uncapped or separately capped, outside the basket. IP warranty that all Company IP is owned/validly licensed, unqualified by this disclosure.

## 11. Privacy incident (cl 4.6, Sch 6; DL para 6)

**Facts:** Download link sent to an unintended external address; ~1,240 records of personal information (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). Unknown whether accessed; investigation preliminary; six weeks old.

**Seller position:** "Preliminary operational matter", not material.

**Analysis:** Under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, the entity must assess a suspected eligible data breach within 30 days of becoming aware of it. The incident was disclosed as at 22 September; it is now 5 November — the 30-day assessment window has lapsed. If the assessment concluded serious harm is likely, notification to the OAIC and affected individuals is mandatory. The Seller's material "does not establish" whether notification is required — which suggests the assessment has not been completed or not been disclosed. Post-2024 reforms, OAIC has a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy and increased civil penalties (up to AUD 50m for serious interferences). The affected individuals also appear to be users of the Company's platform — i.e. customer-side data, raising contractual breach-notification obligations under customer contracts (very likely including Bluefen).

**Recommendation:** Require immediate production of the completed assessment; confirmation whether OAIC/individual/customer notifications were made; forensic evidence of non-access if relied upon. Specific indemnity for all loss arising from the DD-006 incident (regulatory, third-party, notification costs, customer claims), uncapped or capped at price, outside the basket, 6 years. Specific warranty of compliance with Privacy Act and customer data obligations. If notification obligations were missed, that is a current breach of law and should be remediated before Completion.

## 12. Sandbar supplier renewals (DL para 8)

**Facts:** Three related renewals, AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330k), split across DD-008 and DD-011; the Seller does not say whether they are accrued, terminable or ordinary course.

**Analysis:** Three identical amounts across two documents is a pattern worth probing — either a single arrangement deliberately split (below a materiality or approval threshold?) or related-party. The Buyer needs to know if these are committed liabilities at Completion (debt-like / working capital) or genuinely recurring opex priced into the valuation.

**Recommendation:** DD follow-up: copies of all three contracts, counterparties' ownership, approval history. If accrued or non-cancellable at Completion, include in completion-accounts adjustment. Seller warranty that no related-party arrangements exist other than as listed.

## 13. Office lease (DL para 7) and Mossvale (DL para 9)

- **Lease:** a notification obligation is still a Completion deliverable — require evidence it is given, and a warranty that the lease contains no change-of-control termination right. Verify directly.
- **Mossvale:** the Seller's drafting ("does not state consent is required merely because shares are sold") is careful. Review DD-009 ourselves for any change-of-control or "deemed assignment" language; many Australian contracts treat change of control as assignment. Add to the list of contracts for a Seller warranty of no change-of-control triggers.

## 14. Title (DL para 10)

**Analysis:** The share register is prima facie evidence of title under the *Corporations Act 2001* (Cth), but it is not conclusive and the Seller is at pains to say the Buyer has not verified it. The Seller's wish to cap title warranties (item 2) sits uneasily with this. Independent verification needed: ASIC company extract (current members, no charges/PPSR registrations over the shares), copy of the share certificate(s), constitution (pre-emptive rights, transfer restrictions), any shareholders' agreement, options/convertible notes, and historical transfers to Harbourglass.

**Recommendation:** Complete those searches now. Full-cap, long-period title warranty (item 2) is non-negotiable.
